plan: Bid in a second-price (Vickrey) auction with 3 bidders. Truthful bidding is weakly dominant: bid exactly my value. Overbidding risks negative profit if rivals’ highest bid lies between 24 and my inflated bid. Underbidding risks losing profitable wins when rivals’ max bid is below 24. The $0.1 grid doesn’t alter dominance. No history to exploit in a single round. Therefore, bid 24 to maximize expected profit: win whenever the highest competing bid is <24 and pay that price, securing surplus 24 − (highest competing bid).

[ In a second-price auction with independent private values, the weakly dominant strategy is to bid your true value. Overbidding can force paying above value if others bid high; underbidding risks losing profitable wins when others bid below your value. There’s no advantage to shading for tie-breaking since winning at price equal to value yields zero profit anyway. With a private value of $9 and no informative history (single round), bid exactly $9.0 to maximize expected profit. ]

[ This is a sealed-bid second-price auction: if I win, I pay the highest competing bid, not my own. In such auctions, bidding my true value weakly dominates all other strategies—overbidding risks paying above value; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. With value = 13 and no informative history (1 round), optimal long-run and short-run policy is truthful bidding. Tie-breaking is random; bidding exactly 13 preserves optimality. ]
